lessonTitle: Common Out-of-Hours Calls: Chest Pain, Breathlessness, Oliguria, Abnormal Scores and Confusion

blocks.text: It is 03:10 and your bleep goes: a nurse on a surgical ward asks you to see a patient who is 'just not right'. She has a set of observations and a number, but not yet a diagnosis. Out-of-hours calls rarely arrive labelled; your job is to turn a vague worry into a structured assessment within minutes.

blocks.markdown: Most ward calls to a new doctor fall into a small number of patterns: **chest pain**, **breathlessness**, **low urine output**, an **abnormal early warning score**, and a **confused or agitated patient**. The skill is not memorising a diagnosis for each. It is applying the same safe sequence every time: go to the patient, make a rapid ABCDE assessment (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure), treat life-threatening problems as you find them, call for senior help early, and then work out the cause. Doses and local protocols differ between hospitals; anything quoted here is a teaching example, so always check against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

blocks.title: Early warning score (EWS)
blocks.text: A track-and-trigger system that converts routine vital signs into a single aggregate number. Each physiological parameter is scored by how far it lies from normal, and the aggregate (and any single extreme parameter) triggers a graded clinical response. In the NHS in England the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) is widely used; check which version and which trigger thresholds your trust has adopted.

blocks.markdown: **How NEWS2 is built.** Seven items are scored: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, whether the patient is on supplemental oxygen (scores 0 or 2), systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness (new confusion scores the same as voice, pain or unresponsive) and temperature. Each parameter other than oxygen use scores 0 to 3. Oxygen saturation has a separate scale for patients with a target of 88 to 92 percent (for example confirmed hypercapnic respiratory failure); this is set by a clinician, not by the nurse on the night. The aggregate is the sum, and the usual response bands are: 0 to 4 low, 5 to 6 medium (urgent response), 7 or more high (emergency response). **A single parameter scoring 3 also triggers an urgent clinical review even if the aggregate is low.** Confirm the exact bands against the current Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart and local policy.

blocks.caption: The aggregate is a plain sum of the seven item scores s_i, including the 0 or 2 for supplemental oxygen.

blocks.title: Scoring an abnormal set of observations
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old on day 2 after bowel surgery is breathing air with: respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 93 percent, systolic BP 108 mmHg, pulse 96 per minute, alert, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. Calculate the NEWS2 aggregate (scale 1 saturations) and state the response band.

steps.text: Score each parameter against the chart. A respiratory rate of 22 per minute lies in the 21 to 24 band, which scores 2.
SpO2 93 percent lies in the 92 to 93 band (scale 1), which scores 2. The patient is on air, so the oxygen item scores 0.
Systolic BP 108 mmHg lies in the 101 to 110 band, which scores 1. A pulse of 96 lies in the 91 to 110 band, which scores 1.
Alert scores 0 and a temperature of 37.2 degrees Celsius lies in the normal band, which scores 0.
Add the scores in the order respiratory rate, SpO2, oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness, temperature.

An aggregate of 6 is in the medium band, which prompts an urgent response: bedside review by a clinician competent in assessing acute illness, with a decision about frequency of observations and escalation. Check the response bands against local policy.

blocks.answer: NEWS2 = 6 (medium risk): attend promptly, perform an ABCDE assessment, look for the cause (here early respiratory compromise, for example atelectasis, pneumonia or pulmonary embolism) and inform a senior.

blocks.markdown: **Chest pain.** The first question is whether this is a life-threatening cause: acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis with tamponade, or oesophageal rupture. Go to the patient, check ABCDE and the full set of observations, ask about the character, onset, radiation, associated symptoms and risk factors, and record a 12-lead ECG without delay. Pain after surgery or immobility, with pleuritic character, tachycardia or hypoxia, should raise pulmonary embolism. Troponin and other blood tests refine the diagnosis; they must never delay attending the patient or the ECG. Treatment decisions (for example antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy) must follow current local protocols and senior advice.

**Breathlessness.** Look first for airway obstruction, then respiratory rate, work of breathing, saturations and added sounds. Give oxygen to correct hypoxaemia, targeting the saturation range set in the prescription or, if none exists, the generally recommended ranges (commonly 94 to 98 percent, or 88 to 92 percent for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure; check the current British Thoracic Society guideline). Common causes on a ward are pulmonary oedema, pneumonia, COPD or asthma exacerbation, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax and anaphylaxis, and the examination, ECG, chest radiograph and arterial blood gas help to separate them.

rows: ABCDE, observations, analgesia as prescribed and appropriate, senior help
Acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax
12-lead ECG, troponin per protocol, chest radiograph
ABCDE, oxygen to target, sit upright, senior help
Anaphylaxis, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, severe asthma or COPD exacerbation

Check catheter and fluid status, review observations

Bladder scan, urinalysis, urea and electrolytes, fluid balance chart

Hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, alcohol or drug withdrawal, pain, retention, intracranial event

blocks.caption: Four common calls: what to do and what not to miss.

blocks.markdown: **Low urine output (oliguria).** A widely used working threshold is a urine output below 0.5 mL per kg per hour sustained over about 6 hours, which is also used in kidney injury staging; confirm the definition used by your trust. Oliguria is a sign, not a diagnosis. In a catheterised patient, first check that the catheter is not blocked, kinked or displaced, and measure the actual hourly volumes. Then consider pre-renal causes (hypovolaemia, sepsis, haemorrhage, poor cardiac output), renal causes (nephrotoxic drugs, acute tubular injury) and post-renal obstruction. Review the drug chart for nephrotoxic or hypotensive agents, and do not give a large fluid bolus automatically to a patient with heart failure.

blocks.caption: Weight-adjusted urine output; the volume and the time must cover the same period.

blocks.title: Is this urine output low?
blocks.prompt: A catheterised patient weighing 72 kg has produced 150 mL of urine over the last 6 hours. Calculate the output in mL per kg per hour and compare it with a threshold of 0.5 mL per kg per hour.

steps.text: Write the formula: rate equals volume divided by body mass times time. The volume is 150 mL, the mass is 72 kg and the time is 6 h.
Multiply the denominator: 72 kg x 6 h = 432 kg h.
Divide: 150 mL / 432 kg h = 0.347 mL per kg per hour.

Compare: 0.35 is below the 0.5 mL per kg per hour threshold, so this is oliguria. Check the catheter, review the observations and fluid status, and escalate according to the trigger set by local policy.

blocks.answer: About 0.35 mL per kg per hour, which is below 0.5, so oliguria; it needs a prompt assessment of the catheter, volume status and cause.

blocks.markdown: **Confused or agitated patient.** New confusion in an inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise, and is a medical problem with a cause. Look for hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, pain, urinary retention, constipation, medication effects, alcohol or drug withdrawal and metabolic or neurological causes. Use non-drug measures first: a calm, unhurried approach, reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, good lighting, and involving relatives or carers. In England and Wales the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies: assume capacity, but if the patient lacks capacity for a specific decision, any act must be in their best interests and the least restrictive option. Restraint or sedation is a last resort for immediate danger, should follow local policy and senior advice, and doses must be checked against the BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Never anchor on the label 'confusion'
blocks.text: Calling a new change in behaviour 'just their dementia' or 'sundowning' without checking glucose, oxygenation and observations misses treatable and sometimes life-threatening causes. Always exclude hypoglycaemia and hypoxia first, because both are quick to check and quick to treat.

points: Treat every call with the same ABCDE structure before searching for a diagnosis.
An early warning aggregate, and any single parameter scoring 3, triggers a graded response; confirm thresholds with local policy.
Oliguria is below about 0.5 mL per kg per hour over around 6 hours; check the catheter and volume status first.
New confusion is delirium until proven otherwise: exclude hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and sepsis, use non-drug measures and act within the Mental Capacity Act.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on day 3 after an inguinal hernia repair describes central chest pressure with sweating that began 20 minutes ago. Observations: pulse 104 per minute, BP 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 97 percent on air. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.text: Ask the nurse to send a troponin and wait for the result before attending
Reassure him that post-operative pain is common and re-check observations in 4 hours
Attend promptly, perform an ABCDE assessment, record a 12-lead ECG and involve a senior early
Prescribe an antacid for presumed reflux and review in the morning

questions.correctOptionText: Attend promptly, perform an ABCDE assessment, record a 12-lead ECG and involve a senior early

distractorRationale.a: Delays assessment; blood tests support, not replace, bedside review and an ECG.
distractorRationale.b: Under-triages a patient with a worrying symptom and tachycardia.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a potentially cardiac cause must be assessed at the bedside, with an ECG, without waiting for results.
distractorRationale.d: Anchors on a benign cause when a life-threatening one has not been excluded.

questions.explanation: Sweating and central pressure raise the possibility of acute coronary syndrome, and tachycardia in a post-operative patient also keeps pulmonary embolism in play. The safe approach is to see the patient, make an ABCDE assessment, obtain an ECG and call for senior help early; investigations such as troponin follow local protocols and must not delay review.

questions.stem: A septic patient weighing 84 kg has a urinary catheter. The nurse records 190 mL of urine in total over the last 8 hours. Calculate the average urine output in mL per kg per hour.
questions.explanation: Weight-adjusted output is volume divided by body mass times time: 190 / (84 x 8) = 190 / 672, which is approximately 0.283 mL per kg per hour. This is below the usual working threshold of 0.5 mL per kg per hour, so it counts as oliguria and needs assessment of the catheter, fluid status and cause.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with known COPD and a previous episode of hypercapnic respiratory failure is breathless on the ward with SpO2 84 percent on air. Her notes carry an oxygen alert card. What is the most appropriate oxygen strategy while you assess her?

options.text: Give controlled oxygen to a target saturation of 88 to 92 percent and check an arterial blood gas
Give oxygen only if she becomes drowsy
Withhold oxygen entirely because of the risk of carbon dioxide retention
Give high-flow oxygen to bring SpO2 to 100 percent

questions.correctOptionText: Give controlled oxygen to a target saturation of 88 to 92 percent and check an arterial blood gas

distractorRationale.a: Correct: avoids both hypoxaemia and worsening hypercapnia; confirm target with current BTS guidance.
distractorRationale.b: Waiting for a late sign risks avoidable hypoxic injury.
distractorRationale.c: Untreated hypoxaemia is itself dangerous; the aim is controlled, not absent, oxygen.
distractorRationale.d: Over-oxygenation can worsen hypercapnia in at-risk patients.

questions.explanation: Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure should receive titrated oxygen aimed at a lower target range, with 88 to 92 percent being the commonly recommended range, and a blood gas to follow carbon dioxide and pH. Withholding oxygen or giving unlimited oxygen are both unsafe; check the current British Thoracic Society guidance and the patient's own target.

questions.stem: A nurse reports a patient with a NEWS2 aggregate of 3, all of which comes from a systolic blood pressure of 88 mmHg; every other parameter is normal. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the blood pressure in 12 hours
Treat as an emergency and activate a cardiac arrest call
Continue routine observations because the aggregate is only 3
Attend for an urgent clinical review, because a single parameter scoring 3 triggers escalation even when the aggregate is low

questions.correctOptionText: Attend for an urgent clinical review, because a single parameter scoring 3 triggers escalation even when the aggregate is low

distractorRationale.a: Delays review of possible shock or hypovolaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Disproportionate; the patient is not in arrest and an urgent ward-based review is the expected response.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: a single extreme score is a trigger in its own right.

questions.explanation: A systolic pressure of 88 mmHg scores 3 on its own, and NEWS2 teaches that any single parameter scoring 3 should prompt an urgent review by a clinician competent in acute illness even when the aggregate is in the low band. This protects against missing a patient whose deterioration is concentrated in one physiological system; confirm the local escalation policy.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has: respiratory rate 23 per minute, SpO2 94 percent on supplemental oxygen (scale 1), systolic BP 104 mmHg, pulse 112 per minute, alert, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Using the NEWS2 chart, calculate the aggregate score (a whole number).
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate 23 scores 2, SpO2 94 percent scores 1, supplemental oxygen scores 2, systolic BP 104 scores 1, pulse 112 scores 2, alert scores 0 and temperature 38.4 scores 1. The sum is 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 1 = 9, which is in the high band (7 or more) and needs an emergency response, subject to local policy.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man admitted with a urinary tract infection becomes newly agitated overnight and keeps pulling at his cannula. His observations are stable. Which action should come first?

options.text: Attribute it to dementia and ask the nurse to observe
Check a capillary glucose and oxygen saturation and look for other reversible causes such as pain or urinary retention
Prescribe sedation straight away to protect the cannula
Apply physical restraint to prevent harm

questions.correctOptionText: Check a capillary glucose and oxygen saturation and look for other reversible causes such as pain or urinary retention

distractorRationale.a: Anchoring; there is no stated dementia and new confusion needs investigation.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: delirium has treatable causes that must be sought before sedation.
distractorRationale.c: Skips the search for a cause; sedation is a last resort.
distractorRationale.d: The least restrictive option must be tried first and restraint is not first-line.

questions.explanation: New agitation in an older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise, and hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, pain, retention, constipation and infection are common and treatable contributors. Quick bedside checks come first, followed by non-drug measures; sedation and restraint are last resorts under local policy and the Mental Capacity Act.

questions.stem: A 82-year-old woman on a medical ward, previously independent and orientated, is now disorientated, shouting and trying to leave. Her observations are normal and a nurse asks whether to give sedation. Discuss how you would manage her safely.
markingGuide: Recognise probable delirium and treat as a medical problem; avoid labelling as 'just confusion'
Check ABCDE, capillary glucose, oxygen saturation, temperature and pain
Look for causes: infection, urinary retention, constipation, medicines, withdrawal, metabolic or neurological problems
Non-drug measures first: calm approach, reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, lighting, familiar people
Assess capacity for the specific decision; if lacking, act in best interests with the least restrictive option (Mental Capacity Act 2005, England and Wales)
Medication or restraint only if there is immediate risk, following local policy and senior advice, with doses checked in the BNF
Escalate to senior, document findings and plan, and review regularly
questions.explanation: A strong answer treats delirium as a symptom with a cause, secures safety with the least restrictive means, and reserves sedation for immediate danger. It also names the legal framework (capacity and best interests) while recognising that drug choice and dose must be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A new onset of confusion in a patient who was previously alert scores 3 in the consciousness parameter of NEWS2, in the same way as responding only to voice, pain or being unresponsive.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: NEWS2 groups new confusion with voice, pain and unresponsive responses into a single parameter that scores 3, because acute change in mental state is an important sign of physiological deterioration. This is why a patient with new confusion can trigger an urgent review even when the other parameters are normal.

questions.stem: You are called to a patient whose NEWS2 aggregate is 7. Which approach best reflects the usual high-risk response?

options.text: Arrange a routine review on the next ward round
Repeat observations after an hour before deciding what to do
Go immediately, start ABCDE management, and call for an emergency assessment by a team with critical-care competencies
Manage alone and inform the seniors in the morning

questions.correctOptionText: Go immediately, start ABCDE management, and call for an emergency assessment by a team with critical-care competencies

distractorRationale.a: Far too slow for a high aggregate.
distractorRationale.b: Delays a response required at this level of risk.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: high-risk scores warrant emergency senior or critical-care input.
distractorRationale.d: A junior must not manage a high-risk patient without early senior help.

questions.explanation: An aggregate of 7 or more falls in the high-risk band, which calls for an emergency response and continuous monitoring, with assessment by clinicians skilled in critical care. As a new doctor you go to the patient, start first-line management and call for help immediately; always follow the local escalation policy.

questions.stem: A man of 66 is 24 hours after a colectomy. His urinary catheter has drained only 90 mL over the past 6 hours. His pulse is 108 per minute and blood pressure 98/60 mmHg. Outline your assessment of this call and the main causes you would consider.
markingGuide: Attend and perform ABCDE with full observations and early warning score
Check the catheter: blocked, kinked, bag position, flush or bladder scan per protocol
Assess volume status: fluid balance chart, capillary refill, examination, bleeding or ongoing losses
Causes grouped as pre-renal (hypovolaemia, bleeding, sepsis), renal (nephrotoxic drugs, acute tubular injury) and post-renal (obstruction)
Review drug chart for nephrotoxic or antihypertensive drugs and review blood tests including urea and electrolytes
Fluid decisions guided by assessment, with caution in heart failure; escalate to a senior early
questions.explanation: Oliguria with tachycardia and low-normal blood pressure after major surgery suggests hypovolaemia or bleeding until proven otherwise, but a blocked catheter and obstruction must be excluded first. A structured pre-renal, renal and post-renal approach, with early senior review and a fluid plan that reflects volume status, earns the marks.
